title: Interior and Postcards
premise: Xanthe Lockridge, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after a betrayal he never named, has built a career on elegant evasion — reviews that praise everything and mean nothing. When his mother dies and a box of undelivered letters surfaces behind her wardrobe, he discovers she spent decades writing to a man she never sent them to: his supposed father's brother, who ran the old neighborhood's last bus depot. As Xanthe traces the letters' intended recipient through a city being rerouted around him, he must finally translate the one untranslatable sentence his mother left unfinished — a sentence about who he really is — and decide whether love that arrives late is still love. The book ends with Xanthe catching the final bus before the line closes, delivering the last letter himself, and writing his first honest review, which is about his mother's kitchen and tastes, for the first time in five years, like something.
about_author: Emrys Galloway is the pen name of a former food writer who left restaurant journalism after a decade of reviews he no longer believes. They live near a decommissioned bus line and write about inheritance, appetite, and the things families postmark but never send.

chapters.title: The Palate of Ash
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At a lavish tasting menu, Xanthe writes a glowing review of food he cannot taste, his fifth year of professional fraud. A young sous-chef catches his blank stare at the plate. The beat is quiet shame — the reader learns he has forgotten flavor itself, and he has learned to hide it beautifully.

chapters.title: Wardrobe, Rear Panel
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Clearing his dead mother's flat, Xanthe pries loose a warped wardrobe panel and finds a biscuit tin: forty years of letters, all addressed, stamped, never sent — all to a man named Aurel. The beat is vertigo; the mother he mourned becomes a stranger holding a sealed life.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with flashbacks. Xanthe rereads his own archive of reviews and recognizes his mother's technique in himself: the art of almost saying it. He remembers the family silence around his father's brother Aurel, erased from every photograph. The beat is dawning inheritance — evasion is the family trade.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The final letter stops mid-sentence, the ink dragged: 'Your son is not—'. Xanthe becomes obsessed with completing it, reading it in every register. His editor calls about a missed deadline; he lies with practiced grace. The beat is fixation sharpening into need.

chapters.title: Depot Number Nine
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He tracks Aurel to the old neighborhood's bus depot, now slated for closure and rerouting in six weeks. A woman named Sef — Aurel's granddaughter, who drives the last route — tells him Aurel died in spring, waiting for a letter that never came. The beat is grief arriving at the wrong door.

chapters.title: What Sef Kept
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Sef shows Xanthe her grandfather's side of the silence: forty years of unsent replies, kept in a depot locker, written the night of each unsent letter's date. He knew. He always knew. The beat is stunned reciprocity — two people almost-speaking across a lifetime.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A cousin's drunken wedding toast forces the question Xanthe has dodged: was Aurel his father, not the man in the photographs? Xanthe storms out and, in the car park, cannot remember his father's voice. The beat is identity cracking along the fault line of a pronoun.

chapters.title: A Review of Nothing
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. His editor, suspicious, assigns him the depot neighborhood's dying café — a trap or a mercy. Xanthe sits through a meal of nothing special and writes, for the first time, the truth: that the food tastes like waiting. He doesn't file it. The beat is the fraud beginning to fail him.

chapters.title: Letters, Interleaved
chapters.summary: Alternating excerpts, framed by Xanthe's POV. The chapter braids his mother's letters with Aurel's unsent replies across three decades — a love conducted entirely in drafts, each one ending just before the sentence that mattered. The beat is aching tenderness for two people who perfected almost.

chapters.title: The Rerouting
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. The transit authority announces the depot's final service date. Sef fights the closure with petitions nobody signs, and realizes she is fighting for a grandfather's ghost as much as a bus line. She asks Xanthe, bluntly, why he's really here. The beat is confrontation as invitation.

chapters.title: Taste, Returning
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Eating Sef's depot-brewed coffee and burnt toast, Xanthe tastes something for the first time in five years — not flavor exactly, but appetite, want. He is terrified. The beat is hope arriving disguised as a symptom, and the suspicion that feeling returns only when truth does.

chapters.title: My Mother's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, deep flashback. Xanthe reconstructs the original betrayal: as a boy he caught his mother burning Aurel's letters and, when asked, said nothing — choosing his father's household, his own comfort, the lie that held the family together. The beat is the reader understanding the taste he lost was guilt.

chapters.title: The Cousin's Claim
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The cousin produces family documents: Xanthe's inheritance of the flat is contingent on 'the family narrative' staying intact — the letters must be destroyed. Xanthe's livelihood and legacy are priced against the truth. The beat is duty extending its hand, and Xanthe almost taking it.

chapters.title: Sef Reads Her Grandfather
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Sef finally reads the locker letters end to end and finds Aurel's last entry: a request to be buried on the route of the Number Nine, 'so the city has to drive past what it discarded.' She tells Xanthe the sentence his mother couldn't finish may exist — in Aurel's copy of her first letter, annotated. The beat is the plot tightening into a race.

chapters.title: The Annotated Letter
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the locker, they find the annotated letter — but the page bearing Aurel's answer to 'Your son is not—' has been torn out, decades ago, by someone who wanted it unread. Xanthe suspects his mother retrieved it on her one visit to the depot. The beat is betrayal compounding betrayal, inheritance as theft.

chapters.title: What the Cousin Burned
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Confronting the cousin, Xanthe discovers his mother didn't take the page — the cousin's father did, to secure the family name, and the page has sat in a safe-deposit box for thirty years. Xanthe trades his claim on the flat for it, gladly. The beat is the cost of truth revealed as cheaper than feared.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Translated
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Alone at night, Xanthe reads the recovered page: 'Your son is not his father's, and I am glad of it every day, and too much a coward to say it while you could hear me.' The untranslatable sentence turns out to be simple. Xanthe weeps in a bus shelter like a boy. The beat is devastating release.

chapters.title: Living With It
chapters.summary: Xanthe and Sef's alternating POV. Xanthe doesn't rush to publish or accuse; he sits with the sentence, visits his mother's grave, cooks her recipes and finally tastes them. He and Sef grow close without almost-saying anything. The beat is the quiet middle of real change — love practiced, not declared.

chapters.title: The Last Review
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe publishes the review he never filed — the café, the waiting, his own lost tongue — under his real name, and resigns from the column. The fallout is swift and public; the cousin disowns him; his editor, unexpectedly, is moved. The beat is the fraud's funeral and the writer's birth in a single act.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. The closure order stands, but Sef wins one concession: the Number Nine's final run will follow the original route past the depot, past Aurel's grave, past the old flat. She asks Xanthe to ride it with the letters. The beat is the community, small and stubborn, gathering for a farewell.

chapters.title: The Final Bus
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. On the last run, Xanthe delivers all forty years of letters — reading them aloud at each stop to strangers who board to listen, finishing his mother's sentences where she couldn't, ending at Aurel's grave with the words she never sent. The beat is catharsis: the almost-said, finally said, witnessed.

chapters.title: Interior, With Postcards
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. Months later, Xanthe writes a book — this book — from his mother's kitchen table, taste fully returned, sending Sef postcards from every meal that means something. The last image is a stamped, addressed envelope, going out into the world. The beat is resolution: the inheritance of speech, finally delivered.
